Paclitaxel · Olaparib · TPGS micelle · pH-thermosensitive Introduction Ovarian cancer (OC), commonly called the ‘silent killer,’ is inconspicuous at early stages because it is asymptomatic and has a poor prognosis (Matsuo et al. 2014; Menon et al. Stage III cancer cells spread beyond the pelvis and into the abdomen, thus developing into stage IV OC, further complicating its treatment (Agarwal et al. 2003; Slack-Davis et al. In addition, even after chemotherapy, 60–80% of patients with OC experience recurrence due to multi-drug resistance (MDR) (Zhao et al. 2013a; Zhang et al. Among various therapies for OC, pressurized intraperitoneal aerosol chemotherapy (PIPAC) and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) have emerged as effective treatments (Van Driel et al. 2018; Mishra et al. HIPEC circulates anti-cancer drugs heated to approximately 42 °C within the abdominal cavity for approximately 90 min, and is used to eliminate tumors remaining in the abdominal cavity after surgery.
However, HIPEC has several limitations.
Firstly, HIPEC is a complex treatment that combines surgery and chemotherapy, leading to prolonged surgery times which can place a significant physical strain on patients.

The average duration of surgery ranges from 6 to 9 h, and sometimes it may extend even longer (Roviello et al. 2010; Cianci et al. 2019; Yang et al. Secondly, since HIPEC involves the direct injection of high-temperature drugs into the abdominal cavity, it can cause serious complications such as burns, bowel perforations, and intraperitoneal bleeding.

Additionally, the high temperatures may damage intra-abdominal tissues (Bhatt et al.2016; Mehta et al. 2016; Lundbech et al. Lastly, HIPEC requires advanced technology and specialized equipment, limiting the availability of medical facilities that can provide this treatment, and the costs associated with it are very high (Schwartz et al. 2020; Deo et al. PIPAC, introduced as palliative treatment for peritoneal metastases, delivers chemotherapeutic drugs in an aerosol form by maintaining high pressure inside the abdominal cavity.

However, PIPAC has limitations owing to its uneven drug delivery, distribution, and penetration into various parts of the peritoneum (De Andrade et al. 2019; Nadiradze et al. 2019; Park et al. Thus, new treatment strategies are necessary for peritoneal metastases and drug-resistant OC. Paclitaxel (PTX), a well-known agent in the taxane class of chemotherapy drugs, inhibits cancer cell proliferation by targeting microtubules and is extensively applied in the treatment of numerous types of cancer, such as ovarian, breast, and lung cancer (Horwitz 1994; Rowinsky et al. PTX is used as a platinum-based chemotherapy for advanced OC and has led most patients to clinical remission; however, more than 70% of patients experience recurrence (Armstrong et al. Recently, inhibitors targeting the enzyme poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which plays a critical role in the repair of damaged DNA within cells, have surfaced as prospective treatments for recurrent OC (Franzese et al. 2019; Desai et al. These PARP inhibitors improve progression-free survival in patients with breast cancer susceptibility gene (BRCA) mutations (Fong et al. 2009; Jiang et al. Olaparib (OLA) was the first PARP inhibitor to receive approval from the Food and Drug administration and has demonstrated progression-free survival in several trials (Montemorano et al. 2019; Arora et al. However, drug resistance remains an obstacle, and such monotherapies may lead to issues such as tumor heterogeneity, chemotherapy-resistant mutations, and acceleration of tumor recurrence (Hu et al. 2012; Mokhtari et al. Therefore, a combination therapy that overcomes Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:303–319 tumor heterogeneity, reduces anti-cancer drug resistance, and exhibits anti-cancer effects through synergistic effects can be considered a promising strategy for treating OC (Cho et al. 2015; Jo et al. The combination of PTX and PARP inhibitors has been reported previously.

Shi et al. demonstrated further reduction in cell growth and enhanced apoptosis using a combination of PTX and OLA, compared to those with PTX treatment alone in breast cancer Bcap37 cells (Shi et al. Topçul et al. demonstrated that the combination of nab-PTX with a PARP inhibitor significantly reduces cellular, mitotic, and labeling indices in MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 cell lines, suggesting a potentially effective approach for breast cancer treatment (Topçul et al. Zhang et al. showed that a combination of OLA, PTX, and carboplatin enhances disease control, improves serological parameters, reduces recurrence rates, and demonstrates the absence of additional toxic side effects in patients with OC (Zhang et al. In a randomized phase 2 trial of recurrent platinum-sensitive OC, Oza et al. demonstrated significantly improved progression-free survival using OLA maintenance therapy after combination therapy with OLA, PTX, and carboplatin, compared to that with monotherapy (Oza et al. These results predict that the combination of PTX and OLA is synergistic in OC cell lines and will be an effective treatment strategy.
Additionally, to our knowledge, no studies have reported nanoparticle formulations combining PTX and OLA in OC. However, both drugs are poorly soluble, limiting their clinical application.

D-α-Tocopherol polyethylene glycol 1000 succinate (TPGS) is a surfactant that features both a hydrophobic component derived from vitamin E and a hydrophilic polyethylene glycol (PEG) segment, creating an amphiphilic structure.

Due to its exceptional biocompatibility, enhanced drug solubility, and improved drug penetration, TPGS is extensively employed in the formulation of drug delivery mechanisms (Zhang et al. 2012; Guo et al. In particular, TPGS functions as an inhibitor of the activity of ATP-dependent P-glycoprotein (P-gp), a protein responsible for significantly increasing the efflux of anti-cancer drugs from tumor cells (Collnot et al. 2010; Bu et al. 2014; Yan et al. Overexpression of P-gp is a primary factor contributing to MDR (Arts et al. 1999; Assanhou et al. Using TPGS, mitochondrial targeting can cause dysfunction, depleting intracellular ATP. Reducing ATP levels can affect P-gp activity, reducing extracellular drug efflux (Su et al. 2014; Yang et al. Additionally, previous studies have reported that TPGS is effective in overcoming MDR in OC cell lines.

Zhao et al. synthesized TPGS-b-PBAE, a novel dual-function pH-sensitive copolymer, and demonstrated that the synergistic effects of PBAE and TPGS could overcome MDR in tumors (Zhao et al. Bao Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:303–319 et al. synthesized a novel dual-function redox-sensitive prodrug, TPGS-SS-PTX, and demonstrated higher cell necrosis/apoptosis and increased cytotoxicity than the prodrug against MDR cells (Bao et al. Thus, TPGS could be a promising strategy to overcome MDR OC. Local delivery is an alternative to conventional intravenous administration, which has serious systemic side effects such as immunosuppression, cardiac and hepatorenal toxicity, and myelosuppression (Armstrong et al. 2006; Hanada et al. Intraperitoneal (IP) chemotherapy is a promising local delivery regimen which can maintain high local drug concentrations in the peritoneal cavity, reduce the side effects associated with systemic therapy, and reduce systemic exposure to chemotherapeutic drugs (Petignat et al. 2007; Ceelen et al. Among them, thermosensitive hydrogel is a widely used polymer material existing in a liquid state at room temperature and converts to a gel state when exposed to body temperature (Kim et al. However, these hydrogels are limited by uncontrolled drug release within tumors after in vivo administration (Yang et al. 2016; Zhou et al. To address this, effective strategies utilizing low pH of the cancer environment have emerged (Liu et al. The extracellular pH of tumors averages 6.0–7.0, which is lower than the intracellular pH of 7.4 (Vaupel et al. 1989; Oroojalian et al. This low extracellular pH, along with tumor hypoxia, contributes to the progression of cancer to metastasis (Danhier pH-thermosensitive hydrogel mixtures et al. Poly(dimethylaminoethyl methacrylate-comethoxy poly(ethylene glycol), P(DMAEMA-mPEG), is a polymer composed of PEG (a hydrophilic component) and PDMAEMA (a cationic component).

P(DMAEMAmPEG) has the property of ionizing the entire polymer at low pH due to the presence of a tertiary amine at the end of the DMAEMA group, and is sensitive to temperature due to the DMAEMA and PEG units.
Additionally, it may exhibit reduced gelation at low pH because of the ionizable DMAEMA units.
Therefore, these properties may be useful in drug delivery therapy.

In this study, targeting drug-resistant and peritoneal metastatic OC, we prepared an injectable formulation by mixing a TPGS micelle formulation loaded with PTX and OLA with a gel polymer sensitive to pH and temperature (Fig. Additionally, the synergy between PTX and OLA was assessed using the combination index (CI), while the formulation’s physicochemical characteristics, along with in vitro and in vivo studies, were conducted.
Materials and methods Materials DMAEMA-mPEG was obtained from Polyscitech® (West Lafayette, IN, USA).
PTX, OLA, and sorafenib were d-α-tocopherol polyethylene glycol 1000 succinate (TPGS) micelles and acquired from LC Laboratories® (Woburn, MA, USA).
TPGS, Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO), tert-butanol, sodium azide, and bovine serum albumin (BSA) were procured from Sigma–Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA).
Methanol (MeOH), distilled water (DW), acetonitrile (ACN), and ethanol (EtOH) were obtained from Honeywell Burdick & Jackson (Muskegon, MI, USA).
Sodium hydroxide (NaOH, 0.1 N) and hydrochloric acid (HCl, 0.1 N) solutions were provided by Duksan (Seoul, Korea).
Phosphate buffered saline, also known as PBS with a pH of 7.4, was purchased from Gibco® (Waltham, MA, USA).
All the remaining chemicals and solvents utilized were of analytical or chromatographic quality.
Ovarian cancer cell culture HeyA8-MDR cells, a PTX-resistant human OC cell line, were generously provided by Dr. Jeong Won Lee from Samsung Medical Center in South Korea.
HeyA8-MDR cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium from the Roswell Park Memorial Institute, within a CO incubator maintained at 37 °C and an atmosphere of 5% CO .
The cultivation medium was supplemented with a mixture of penicillin and streptomycin at a concentration of 1% (w/v), along with fetal bovine serum at a 10% (v/v).
Additionally, HeyA8-MDR cells were treated with 300 ng/mL PTX every two weeks, to maintain the characteristic of the ovarian cancer cell line.
Every cell culture product was obtained from Corning, Inc. (Corning, NY, USA).

High–performance liquid chromatography analysis PTX, OLA, and sorafenib (internal standard, IS) concentrations were assessed with a Waters high–performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system (Milford, MA, USA) featuring a 2996 photodiode array detector and a 2695 separation module.

Analysis was performed using a Fortis C18 column (5 μm, 4.6 × 250 mm) set at 30 °C. The sample (10 µL) was injected using an isocratic elution method for PTX, OLA, and IS. The mobile phase was composed of a 70:30 (v/v) ratio of ACN to DW, with a flow rate set at 1.0 mL/ min. The detection wavelengths for PTX, OLA, and IS were 227, 275, and 264 nm, respectively.
The corresponding retention times were 5.8, 2.9, and 9.0 min, respectively.
Drug levels were quantified by matching peak areas to a calibration curve.
Combination index analysis The interaction between PTX and OLA was assessed using a CI analytical approach based on the method developed by Chou (Chou 20.

The CI was calculated as follows: Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:303–319 (D) (D) Combinationindex (CI)= 1 + 2 (D ) (D ) x 1 x 2 Here, (D) and (D) represent the 50% inhibitory concentrations (IC ) of PTX (drug 1) and OLA (drug 2), respectively, when combined.
In contrast, (D ) and (D ) indicate the x 1 x 2 IC values of each individual drug.
A CI value less than 1 signified synergism, a value of 1 represented additive effects, and a value greater than 1 indicated antagonism.

Preparation of PTX/OLA-loaded TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogel mixtures PTX/OLA-loaded TPGS micelles were prepared by freezedrying (Kasper et al. Various ratios of PTX and OLA were weighed into scintillation vials along with the TPGS polymer (12.5, 25, or 50 mg).
A vial containing 1 mL of tert-butanol was submerged in a water bath at 60 °C and agitated for dissolution, then subjected to sonication for 30 min to ensure the drug was fully dissolved.
Subsequently, 1 mL PBS (pH 7. pre-warmed in the water bath was added, followed by vortexing.
This mixture was then rapidly frozen at -70 °C for 1 h and lyophilized for 24 h using an Advantage Pro freeze dryer (SP Scientific, Warminster, PA, USA).

Following this, the lyophilized cake was rehydrated using 1 mL PBS (pH 7. pre-warmed in a water bath at 60 °C. The solution containing PTX/OLA in TPGS micelles was spun for 5 min at 13,000 rpm and 4 °C using a high speed centrifuge (Hanil Science Inc., Gimpo, Korea), and the resulting clear liquid was passed through a sterile 0.2 μm filter (Corning, NY, USA).
Next, the PTX/OLA-loaded TPGS micelles and pHthermosensitive hydrogel mixtures were prepared.

A micellar solution was initially added to the P(DMAEMA-mPEG) polymer and rehydrated at 4 °C for 48 h. Then, the combined sample underwent centrifugation at 13,000 rpm for 5 min with a high speed centrifuge (SciLab®, Seoul, Korea).

Phase transition measurement of PTX/OLA-loaded TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogel mixtures The temperatures at which the micelle-gel mixture and the blank P(DMAEMA-mPEG) gel (vehicle) undergo phase transitions were determined by employing the vial inversion test (Shi et al. 2016; Karunakaran et al. The phase transition temperatures were evaluated at different concentrations of 10, 12.5, and 15% w/v. 0.5 mL of the gel was positioned in the base of a scintillation vial and visually inspected on a hot plate stirrer, inverting the vial after every increase of 1 °C. Gelation was identified by the lack Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:303–319 of movement for 30 s following the inversion of the vial.
Each sample was analyzed at least in triplicates.

Evaluating the physicochemical characteristics of TPGS micelles and mixtures of TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogels The zeta potential, particle size, and polydispersity index (PDI) of PTX/OLA-loaded TPGS micelles and mixtures of PTX/OLA-loaded TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogels were assessed using Litesizer dynamic light scattering (DLS) 500 (Anton Paar, Graz, Austria).
The samples underwent a 1/10 dilution with PBS (pH 7. prior to measurement.

The drug content loaded into the micelles and gels was analyzed using HPLC after a 1/10 dilution with ACN. The calculations for drug loading (DL%) and encapsulation efficiency (EE%) of PTX and OLA were performed using the following equations (Sun et al. 20: drugweightindrug loadedmicellesandgels EE%= − 100 weightofdruginfeeding × drugweightindrug loadedmicellesandgels DL%= − 100 weightofdrug loadedmicellesandgels × ( − ) The structure of PTX/OLA-loaded TPGS micelles and pHthermosensitive hydrogel mixtures was verified using transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEOL Ltd., Tokyo, Japan).

Pre-treatment for TEM analysis was performed by dropping a 1/10 diluted sample with DW in the center of a copper grid, drying it at 25 °C for 12 h, and measuring it at a voltage of 200 kV. In vitro stability test Stability tests of PTX/OLA-loaded TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogel mixtures were evaluated for two weeks at 4 °C. At intervals of 0, 1, 2, 4, 7, 10, and 14 days, 20 µL samples were withdrawn and diluted 1/50 in PBS (pH 7..

Subsequently, the PDI and particle size were determined through DLS. In vitro cytotoxicity assay The cytotoxicities of various formulations in HeyA8- MDR cells were evaluated using the 3-[4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl]-2,5 diphenyl tetrazolium bromide (MTT) assay (van Meerloo et al. 4000 cells of HeyA8-MDR cells were plated per well in 96-well plates and cultured at 37 °C for 24 h. After removing the RPMI medium, the cells underwent treatment with single and combined free drugs, single and combined methoxy-poly(ethylene glycol)poly(ε-caprolactone) (mPEG-PCL) micelles, or single and combined TPGS micelles.

The drug-free RPMI medium was used as a control. 100 µL of DMSO was used to solubilize the free drug, which was subsequently diluted 1000 times with RPMI medium to exclude DMSO toxicity before use. The micelle formulation containing the drug was diluted 10 times using RPMI medium.

After 48 h, the medium in each well was replaced with 100 µL of MTT solution, which had been previously diluted 10 times with RPMI medium, and then cultured for 4 h. Following the removal of the MTT solution, 100 µL of DMSO was dispensed into every well and then shaken on an NB-101 S orbital shaker (N-BIOTEK, Bucheon, Korea) at 200 rpm for 10 min. The absorbance at 540 nm was determined with a Spectra Max ID3 microplate reader (Molecular Devices, San Jose, CA, USA).
Data analysis was conducted with GraphPad Prism software V8.0 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA).

In vitro drug release assay The release patterns of PTX and OLA from PTX/OLAloaded TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogel mixtures were determined according to methods described in previous studies and evaluated at various pH levels (pH 7.4, 6.5, and 5. (Yu et al. 2013; Chen et al. Briefly, a 0.5 mL sample was deposited at the base of a 10 mL scintillation vial and subjected to incubation in a water bath at 37 °C for 10 min, resulting in gel formation.

Subsequently, each vial was supplemented with 5.0 mL of PBS (pH 7.4, 6.5, or 5. that included 0.03% sodium azide and 2% BSA, and then shaken slowly at 50 rpm and 37 °C. At each time of sampling (0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 24, 48, and 72 h), 100 µL sample was taken and an equal volume of ACN and 50 µL of IS were added.
After vortexing and centrifuging the mixture for 5 min at 13,000 rpm, the supernatant was passed through a 0.2 μm sterile filter.
Subsequently, PTX and OLA concentrations were analyzed using HPLC.
Fresh media was substituted for PBS at every sample interval.
The firstorder model in GraphPad Prism V8.0 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA) was used to evaluate the data.

In vitro cellular uptake assay A cellular uptake assay using coumarin 6 was performed as described previously (Zhang et al. 2006; Anbharasi et al. 2010; Muthu et al. HeyA8-MDR cells were cultured in black 96-well plates with a seeding density of 10 × 104 cells/well.
Following a 24 h period, the cells were subjected to treatment using 100 µL TPGS or mPEG-PCL micelles that were loaded with coumarin 6 (at a drug concentration of 60 µg/mL).

The samples were then evaluated at 2, 4, 6, 8, and 24 h. At the specified intervals, the micelle solutions were rinsed twice using 50 µL of pre-heated PBS. Following this, 50 µL of 0.5% Triton X-100 dissolved in 0.2 N NaOH was added to lyse the cells.
Subsequently, the samples were gently shaken at 30 rpm for 15 min using an NB-101SRC orbital shaker (N-BIOTEK, Bucheon, Korea) in a 37 °C incubator.
Using a microplate reader, the fluorescence intensity of each sample was measured at 480 nm for excitation and 580 nm for emission wavelengths, respectively.

Preparation and cytotoxicity assay using HeyA8- MDR tumor spheroids Considering that cancer cells possess stem cell-like properties, HeyA8-MDR tumor spheroids were prepared as described previously (Shackleton 2010; Ishiguro et al. 2017; Kwak et al. Briefly, 10 µL matrigel (Corning, NY, USA) was dispensed into a Corning® 100 mm ultra-lowattachment culture dish, and 3 µL (3.21 × 104 cells/µL) of cell suspension was seeded into the matrigel.
Samples were cultured for 24 h in a 37 °C incubator, then transferred onto an orbital shaker (NB–101SRC) and cultured for 2 weeks to form spherical tumor spheroids.

The cytotoxic effects of TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogel mixtures loaded with single or combination drugs on HeyA8-MDR tumor spheroids were evaluated using a modified method (Kwak et al. The mature HeyA8-MDR tumor spheroid was positioned on a Corning® transwell and 150 µL of gel was dispensed into 12-well plates.
HeyA8-MDR tumor spheroids were treated with the gel on day 0, and the control group was switched to new medium on days 2 and 5.
For cell staining on days 0 and 7, 100 µL of staining solution (LIVE/DEAD Cell Imaging Kit, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and each sample were placed in a black 96-well plate.
Staining was performed in a 37 °C incubator for 15 min. The area (mm and the region of interest were determined using an In Vivo Imaging System (IVIS; VISQUE In Vivo Smart-LF, Anyang, Korea).

In vivo gel observation and drug release The administration volume for the in vivo drug release test was determined from the data obtained for the toxicity assay.

After one week of acclimatization, ICR mice (female, 7-week-old) were divided into three groups (PTX-loaded TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogel mixture, OLA-loaded TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogel mixture, and PTX/OLA-loaded TPGS micelles and pH-thermosensitive hydrogel mixture).
Approximately 0.2 mL of gel was administered intraperitoneally to each group of mice.
At 15, 30, 60, 120, and 180 min after administration, the mice were euthanized with CO , and the gel was extracted via an abdominal incision to assess the degree of release into the abdominal cavity.
The collected gel was dissolved in ACN, vortexed, centrifuged for 5 min at 13,000 rpm, and the resulting supernatant was passed through a 0.2 μm sterilizing filter.
Each drug’s concentration was quantified using HPLC.
Statistical analysis All results are displayed as the average ± standard deviation (SD).
Each experiment was performed at least thrice.
For statistical evaluation, we used an unpaired t-test (Graph- Pad Prism v. 8.0; GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA, USA).
A p-value below 0.05 was deemed to indicate statistical significance.

Results Evaluating the synergistic effect of PTX and OLA in HeyA8-MDR cells The synergy between PTX and OLA was evaluated using the IC and CI values at different molar ratios of PTX and OLA. As shown in Table 1, the CI value was < 1 for all ratios, showing synergy at all ratios.

Among these, considering the animal administration doses of PTX and OLA, ratios of 1:2, 1:4, and 1:10 were selected and used to manufacture Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:303–319 micelles (Sharma et al. 1996; Auzenne et al. 2007; Santiago- O’Farrill et al. 2020; Sun et al. Physicochemical characterization of TPGS micelles and mixtures of TPGS micelles and pHthermosensitive hydrogels To optimize the final formulation, we first evaluated the physicochemical properties of TPGS micelles.
Among the three ratios evaluated with different amounts of TPGS, the EE (%) of PTX and OLA was the highest (87.9 ± 1.97 and 90.9 ± 4.21, respectively) at a 1:4 ratio using 50 mg TPGS.
Additionally, the PDI value was the lowest at 0.05 ± 0.01 (Table 2).
Therefore, a 1:4 ratio of PTX to OLA, using 50 mg of TPGS, was identified as optimum for use in the final formulation.
Next, the final micelles and pH-thermosensitive gel polymer were mixed, and the gelation and destruction temperatures were evaluated at various polymer concentrations.
Gel formation was absent at 10% w/v, and the gelation temperatures of 12.5% and 15% w/v were 31.7 ± 1.53 °C and 30.0 ± 1.00 °C, respectively.

Additionally, the destruction temperatures were 43.7 ± 2.08 °C and 41.7 ± 0.58 °C, respectively (Fig. Both concentrations formed a gel; however, viscosity of the 15% w/v was too high, and was considered to be unfeasible for future administration.

Therefore, the final polymer concentration was set at 12.5% w/v. In addition, the gelation and destruction temperature of the blank gel at 12.5% w/v were 37.0 ± 1.00 and 41.7 ± 0.58, respectively, exhibiting a significant difference compared to the gelation temperature of the final formulation (Fig. Evaluation of the physicochemical characteristics of the final formulation showed that both drugs had an EE (%) of > 80% and particle size < 30 nm (Table 3).
These formulations were used for the subsequent in vitro and in vivo experiments.

In vivo toxicity test In vivo toxicity studies in ICR mice were performed using various doses of the final formulation (Fig. Mice administered both 60.0 mg/kg and 44.4 mg/kg of the formulation died 1 h after the administration.

Those administered the 20.3 mg/kg dose showed a survival rate of 33.3% until 2 h after administration, but all mice died after 3 h. Mice administered 10.7 mg/kg of the formulation showed a 25% survival rate up to 3 h after administration, but all mice died after 4 h. Those administered the 4.79 mg/kg dose showed a survival rate of 25% at 4 h after administration, but all mice died 5 h later.
Therefore, the final formulation was considered toxic, which appeared to be a result of gel polymer toxicity.

On diagnosis, it is likely to have already metastasized to the peritoneum (Nash et al. Additionally, the problem of recurrence cannot be avoided even after surgery and chemotherapy.
To overcome peritoneal metastasis and drug-resistant OC, we designed a topically administered formulation combining PTX- and OLA-loaded TPGS micelles with pH- and temperature-sensitive gel polymers.
This formulation has the property of remaining in a liquid state at 4 °C and forming a gel at approximately 37 °C, which is the body temperature.
The formed gel is corroded by the low pH of the cancerous area, and the micelles are initially released.

Therefore, the formulation was designed based on the hypothesis that PTX and OLA, possessing different mechanisms of action, accumulate in cells and induce apoptosis.

Using the IC values at various ratios, CI was assessed in HeyA8-MDR cells to determine the synergistic effects of PTX and OLA. As a result, all ratios showed a synergistic effect, and considering the animal administration dose, ratios of 1:2, 1:4, and 1:10 were used to manufacture micelles.
The micelles used in the final formulation were selected at a PTX to OLA ratio of 1:4 using 50 mg of TPGS, showing the highest EE (%) of the two drugs and the lowest PDI value.
Subsequently, the micelle and gel mixtures were evaluated to determine the optimal transition temperature, and 12.5% w/v was determined as the optimum polymer concentration.

In addition, the gelation temperature of the final formulation was approximately 5.3 °C Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 55:303–319 lower than that of the blank gel, possibly due to increase in the PEG portion on mixing of the micelles and gel. The decline in gelation temperature as the PEG content rises could be explained by the following factors: depletion attraction due to the presence of PEG chains, reduction in the volume phase transition temperature of microgels, and PEG inhibiting a lower critical solution temperature (LCST) by causing alignment of water molecules (Moeinzadeh et al. 2011; Cheng et al. 2012; Bain et al. The stability test results confirmed that the final formulation was stable for 2 weeks with a size of less than 30 nm and a PDI value of less than 0.3 at 4 °C. These results indicate that TPGS micelles have the highest cytotoxic effect compared to the free drug and mPEG-PCL micelles (control group).
The in vitro cellular uptake analysis revealed that TPGS micelles had a higher fluorescence intensity than that of the control (mPEG-PCL micelles), and that coumarin expression increased over time.

This indicates that TPGS can increase the cellular uptake efficiency and effectively promote drug accumulation by a receptor-mediated active targeting mechanism (Wang et al. 2013; Zhao et al. These results indicate that the final formulation showed a pH-dependent release pattern and may be effective for targeted cancer therapy (Shenoy et al. 2005; Chen et al. 2011; Wu et al. The in vivo drug release profile was similar to the in vitro release results, with PTX in both single and combination formulations having a slower release rate than that of OLA. After 15 min, 78.5% of PTX was released from the combination formulation, whereas 90.7% of OLA was released.
Additionally, all formulations showed > 95% release of both the drugs after 2 h, indicating that they had decomposed and disappeared.

This data represents the measurement of the remaining drug in the gel after the micelles have exited, suggesting that it may more accurately be described as the release of micelle-encapsulated drugs from the gel, rather than mere drug release.
Therefore, upon comparing in vitro and in vivo release, we observed that in vivo release is faster than in vitro release.
These results may be due to significant differences between in vivo and in vitro conditions and multiple physiological factors.

First, peritoneal fluid contains a various enzymes which can degrade materials that are biologically derived or sensitive to enzymatic degradation; therefore, gel degradation may be affected by enzyme activity (Elmowafy et al. Second, foreign substances such as gels can trigger an immune response by recruiting immune cells which can degrade or encapsulate the material (Capobianco et al. Finally, constant renewal of the peritoneal fluid and intra-abdominal peristalsis can lead to rapid gel erosion (Shin et al. 2017; He et al. Existing two-dimensional monolayer cell models have been used to evaluate the cytotoxicity of anti-cancer drugs; however, they have limitations in mimicking the complex in vivo tumor microenvironment (Lei et al. 2021; Wang et al. Therefore, we evaluated the in vitro antitumor effects using tumor spheroids, an emerging and promising 3D tumor model.

Evaluation of the changes in tumor spheroids prepared with HeyA8-MDR cells for a week revealed that the formulation combining PTX and OLA showed the highest cytotoxic effect relative to the other groups at 7 days.
These results can be attributed to the synergistic interaction of the two drugs in the combination formulation, as shown using CI analysis.
In an in vivo toxicity test, the final formulation showed toxicity even at the lowest evaluated dose of 4.79 mg/kg, and the final formulation was considered toxic.
This toxicity appears to be due to the toxicity of P(DMAEMA-mPEG), which was used as the gel polymer.

These polymers are composed in a 95:5 (DMAEMA: mPEG) ratio and are considered toxic because of the high proportion of DMAEMA (van de Wetering et al. 1997; Van de Wetering et al. Additionally, to our knowledge, the use of P(DMAEMA-mPEG) has not been reported earlier.

Cationic polymers, such as DMAEMA, have been extensively studied as gene and drug delivery systems because of their advantages such as high cellular internalization (Verbaan et al. 2005; Karanikolopoulos et al. 2010; Jia et al. In particular, DMAEMA contains a tertiary amino group and is protonated in acidic solutions (Şen et al. 2005; Gao et al. Despite these benefits the high cytotoxicity of DMAEMA remains a challenge (You et al. 2007; Yu et al. Therefore, the cytotoxicity reported in the present study could also be due to the strong toxicity of DMAEMA.

Although application of the synthesized P(DMAEMA-mPEG) polymer for gene delivery has been reported previously, no research has been conducted on drug delivery systems in vivo (Lin et al. 2008; Valimaki et al. Therefore, to our knowledge, this study is the first in vivo study performed using the P(DMAEMAmPEG) polymer.
The final formulation using P(DMAEMAmPEG) polymer mixed with TPGS micelles showed excellent antitumor effects and pH-dependent release patterns in vitro.
However, the toxicity of these polymers should be addressed, and it is necessary to further explore methods for its clinical applicability.

Conclusion In this study, we prepared new formulation combining TPGS micelle formulations loaded with PTX and OLA with pH- and temperature-sensitive gel polymers to overcome the limitation of peritoneal metastasis and drug-resistant OC. As a result of CI analysis in HeyA8-MDR cells, PTX and OLA showed a synergistic effect at all ratios.
Among them, considering various physicochemical properties, a 1:4 ratio of PTX and OLA using 50 mg of TPGS and a gel polymer concentration of 12.5% w/v were decided as the final formulation.
As a result of the in vitro stability test, it was confirmed that the final formulation was stable at 4 °C for 2 weeks and maintained the sol-gel transition depending on temperature.
In vitro cytotoxicity assays showed that TPGS micelles showed the highest cytotoxic effect than free drug and mPEG-PCL micelles (control).
These results can be attributed to TPGS increasing cellular uptake efficiency, as shown in the cell uptake assay.
In vitro drug release profiles showed that both PTX and OLA showed a pH-dependent release pattern, with the slowest release at pH 7.4.

Additionally, the in vitro and in vivo drug release profiles showed similar release patterns, with PTX showing slower release than OLA. The in vitro antitumor effect using tumor spheroids showed that the final formulation showed the highest cytotoxicity compared to the single formulation.

However, despite the multiple advantages of these formulations, the question of in vivo toxicity remains an important issue that needs to be addressed in future studies. 1 0 0 7 / s 4 0 0 0 5 - 0 2 4 - 0 0 7 0 5 - 7 .
